catalog_quote: Stress is contrastive in Takestani words and partly predictable from word class and shape. Stress in nouns is generally ultimate (e.g., /peˈrʌ/ ‘brother’) unless in nouns ending with the feminine suffix -ɛ (e.g., /zɛjˈni.ɛ/ ‘woman’). Most adverbs and adjectives, like nouns, are stressed on their last syllable, such as [pøland-pøˈland] ‘loud-loud (loudly)’ and [qaˈʃank] ‘beautiful.’ Adpositions are primarily mono-syllabic and are typically cliticized to a nominal complement, which is stressed. An example is the noun-postposition – [zʌˈrine rʌ] ‘child for (for the child)’ in which the nominal component [zʌˈrin] rather than the adposition rʌ is stressed. At the phrase level, nouns attract stress, so adverbs and adjectives are typically less prominent overall. ... Stress assignment in verbs depends on the presence of specific morpho-syntactic features or stress-attracting morphemes that compete for stress in a hierarchy. For example, present tense verbs are generally stressed on their last syllable (e.g., [meχanˈte] ‘laugh.3SG.M.IND (He laughs)’, and past tense verbs are stressed on their stem /ʌˈχɑrtem/ ‘PV.drink.PST.1SG (I drank)’. The interfaces with morphology for stress assignment of verbs go beyond the scope of this study. [p. 570] There are some examples of minimal pairs that directly contrast stress between final and non-final position, such as the nouns /vɛˈjɛ/ ‘wedding’ and /ˈvɛj-ɛ/ ‘bride’ or the verbs /uˈvaz/ ‘dancer’ and /ˈuvaz/ ‘dance!’.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final syllable (nouns, adjectives, adverbs, present-tense verbs); the feminine suffix -ɛ is unstressed so feminine nouns are stressed on the penult; past-tense verbs stress the stem; monosyllabic adpositions are clitics and unstressed. Stress is therefore morphologically conditioned and contrastive in a few morphological minimal pairs (/vɛˈjɛ/ 'wedding' vs /ˈvɛj-ɛ/ 'bride'; /uˈvaz/ 'dancer' vs /ˈuvaz/ 'dance!'), but the placement is predictable from word class and morphology. Yar-Shater 1969 (§§82-83, pp. 57-58) agrees for the whole Southern Tati group: 'All uninflected masculine nouns are stressed on the final syllable'; 'All plural oblique nouns are stressed on the final syllable'; stress 'distinctive' yet 'generally predictable', and 'weak and dominated by sentence stress and intonation'.
new_statements.exceptions: Feminine nouns in -ɛ (older -a) stressed on the penult; past-tense verbs stem-stressed; adpositions cliticized and unstressed; verb stress governed by 'stress-attracting morphemes that compete for stress in a hierarchy' (details declared beyond the study's scope); Yar-Shater 1969: compounds keep only the second member's stress; imperfect stresses the last syllable of the past stem.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, with a note that at phrase level nouns attract stress and adjectives/adverbs are less prominent; Yar-Shater 1969 says word stress is weak and dominated by sentence stress and intonation. Acoustic cues (JIPA): higher f0 and intensity on stressed vowels; duration is not a cue (final lengthening instead).
new_statements.identity_note: The JIPA illustration describes the Takestani dialect of Southern Tati as spoken in the city of Takestan (Siyaden), Qazvin province — exactly Glottolog take1255 / ISO tks. Yar-Shater 1969 states its stress rules for 'Southern Tati' as a group (Chali, Takestani, Eshtehardi, Esfarvarini, Xiaraji, Xoznini, Danesfani, Ebrahimabadi, Sagzabadi) with Takestani examples; Glottolog/Ethnologue subsume this Ramand-Eshtehard group under take1255, so the two sources describe the same variety at different granularity.

sources.quote: Feminine nouns are commonly marked by an unstressed -a, with the stress regularly falling on the penultimate syllable, e.g. Esh. xoza ... Tak. vu(y)a "water", kasuya "turtle", fareka "chicken", hoya "stream". [...] In the masc. nouns the sg. obl. ends in an unstressed -e.
sources.locator: printed p. 242, section (1) Distinction of gender; obl. -e remark printed p. 243, section (2) on the oblique case; footnote 4 p. 242: 'In Cal a number of fem.…
sources.note: Only a partial statement, no general word-stress rule: the feminine marker -a and the masc. sg. oblique -e are unstressed, so stress in fem. nouns sits on the penult (= stem-final syllable). Consistent with the catalog's 'morphological' kind (suffix-sensitive stress) and fills in one concrete rule where the catalog rule field is empty. Nothing on secondary stress, syllable weight, domain, verbal stress or exceptions; no tone mentioned (consistent with no-tone). Statement covers the Ramandi dialects as a group with examples from Esh., Xia., Cal. and Tak.
